title: Offshore Atlantic rapid-intensification window and storm rates showed no clear change between 1982-2002 and 2003-2023
abstract: We tested whether a change in rapid-intensification windows came from more storms with such windows or from longer runs of overlapping windows. We used IBTrACS v04r01 North Atlantic tracks. Each 24-hour window had five six-hour fixes with tropical storm or hurricane status and distance to land of at least 150 km. Rapid intensification meant a wind gain of at least 30 kt. In 1982-2002, 166 of 2,534 eligible windows met this rule. In 2003-2023, 252 of 3,483 windows met it. The rate ratio was 1.10, with a 95% year-bootstrap interval of 0.79 to 1.57. The fraction of eligible storms with rapid intensification fell from 31.4% to 29.8%; its ratio was 0.95 (0.73 to 1.28). Mean windows per run rose from 2.59 to 2.93; its ratio was 1.13 (0.94 to 1.37). Thus, longer runs gave the largest positive factor in an exact rate identity, but none of the primary changes was resolved. A 35 kt fixed-opportunity check gave a positive interval and shows threshold dependence. This is a restricted-sample benchmark, not evidence against broader intensification trends. Runs are not independent physical events. Changes in observations, storm mix and climate variability limit inference. The package has a source subset, code, all results, a figure and an independent count audit.
